qs.q: A 70-year-old man undergoes an emergency total gastrectomy for a perforated gastric ulcer. Post-operatively, he develops a megaloblastic anaemia several years later. The primary site of absorption for the deficient nutrient is located where?
qs.e: Vitamin B12 requires intrinsic factor produced by gastric parietal cells for active receptor-mediated absorption within the terminal ileum.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Surgery Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic steatorrhea and weight loss following a total gastrectomy. Which physiological mechanism best explains his fat malabsorption?
o: Accelerated transit time of lipids through the proximal jejunum
Impaired micelle formation resulting from inadequate bile acids
Deficient secretion of pancreatic lipase via vagal nerve loss
Loss of intrinsic factor preventing normal ileal fat uptake
Decreased brush border lactase activity within the ileum
qs.e: Gastrectomy eliminates the cephalic and gastric phases of pancreatic stimulation, leading to deficient lipase secretion and fat malabsorption.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 50-year-old man who had a Billroth II gastrectomy five years ago presents with recurrent epigastric pain. Endoscopy reveals a marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis. What is the most common underlying mechanism?
o: Inadequate acid reduction or retained gastrin tissue
Permanent bacterial colonization of the afferent jejunal loop
Rapid transit of food causing severe reactive hypoglycaemia
Complete absence of alkaline pancreatic secretions in the stomach
qs.e: Recurrent ulcers, known as marginal ulcers, typically occur at the anastomotic site due to incomplete acid reduction or retained antral tissue. They are distinct from dumping syndrome and bile reflux.
qs.s: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Its Surgical Complications: MCQs

qs.q: A 55-year-old woman who underwent a subtotal gastrectomy two years ago presents with fatigue, pallor, and a macrocytic anaemia. Which nutrient deficiencies are most expected following this surgery?
qs.e: Post-gastrectomy complications commonly include anaemia caused by iron and vitamin B12 deficiency. Osteoporosis is another long-term metabolic complication.
qs.s: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Its Surgical Complications: MCQs

qs.q: A 67-year-old man is diagnosed with a stump carcinoma during routine follow-up. Approximately how many years after his initial partial gastrectomy for peptic ulcer disease does this late complication typically manifest?
qs.e: Stump carcinoma is a well-documented late complication that typically arises 15 to 20 years after gastric surgery for peptic ulcer disease. Early complications relate more to motility or acute metabolic shifts.
qs.s: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Its Surgical Complications: MCQs

qs.q: A 64-year-old man undergoes a subtotal gastrectomy for an antral gastric adenocarcinoma. To ensure an adequate proximal clearance margin in the unstretched stomach, what is the recommended distance of normal tissue required?
o: Requiring a minimum of 15 cm of normal proximal tissue
Maintaining exactly 2 cm of distance from the tumor edge
Requiring at least 5 cm, ideally 8 to 10 cm of tissue
Maintaining between 1 and 3 cm of healthy mucosal tissue
qs.e: Curative surgery requires a clear margin of at least 5 cm, and ideally 8 to 10 cm of normal stomach proximal to the tumour in the unstretched stomach. Shorter margins risk leaving microscopic residual disease that is detrimental to survival.
qs.s: Gastric Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Gastrectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 56-year-old man with a history of a partial gastrectomy performed 18 years ago for peptic ulcer disease presents with a new gastric stump cancer. What is the primary proposed mechanism for this delayed malignancy?
o: Bile reflux into the gastric remnant
High dietary intake of vitamin C
qs.e: Previous partial gastrectomy can lead to stump cancer 15 to 20 years later primarily driven by chronic bile reflux. Helicobacter pylori is common in primary gastric cancer but stump carcinogenesis is heavily influenced by reflux.
qs.s: Gastric Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Gastrectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 61-year-old man with a tumour located in the cardia undergoes a total gastrectomy. What specialized reconstruction technique is employed to prevent bile reflux into the oesophagus?
qs.e: Total gastrectomy is reconstructed with a Roux-en-Y oesophagojejunostomy utilizing a 60 cm Roux limb to effectively prevent bile reflux. Billroth reconstructions are typically used for distal subtotal resections.
qs.s: Gastric Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Gastrectomy: MCQs

ai.title: Gastrectomy
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Gastrectomy is the surgical removal of part or all of the stomach, usually for cancer, peptic ulcer or severe reflux. Post‑operative care focuses on nutrition, acid control and monitoring for complications such as leak, bleeding or dumping syndrome.

sections.p: Gastrectomy is any resection of the stomach. Diagnosis of the underlying disease (gastric cancer, ulcer, reflux) is made by endoscopy with biopsy, imaging and histology.
Staging depends on the underlying pathology. For cancer, the TNM system is used; for ulcers, the Borrmann classification guides extent of resection.
In East Africa the leading indications are gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease (often H. pylori‑related) and severe reflux disease.
Patients may have dysphagia, early satiety, weight loss, epigastric pain, vomiting or bleeding. Post‑operative symptoms include nausea, early dumping, dehydration and protein loss.
Pre‑op workup includes endoscopy, biopsy, CT abdomen, blood tests and nutritional assessment. Post‑op monitoring focuses on haemoglobin, electrolytes and weight.

t.b: Shows ulcer, tumour or reflux changes; biopsy confirms diagnosis
Stages cancer, detects metastasis or complications
Screen for post‑op bleeding when endoscopy unavailable

sections.p: Early complications: anastomotic leak, bleeding, infection, gastric outlet obstruction. Late complications: dumping syndrome, malabsorption, bile reflux gastritis, stump cancer.

Treat the underlying cause first. Post‑op care includes proton‑pump inhibitors, nutritional support (oral or enteral), monitoring for dumping and early mobilisation. Avoid NSAIDs and antiplatelets unless necessary.
Regular endoscopy at 6–12 months post‑op to detect stump cancer or recurrence. Vaccinate against hepatitis B, treat H. pylori, counsel on diet and avoid smoking.
Gastric ulcer, gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease, reflux oesophagitis, and functional dyspepsia.
Post‑op hypoalbuminaemia may be falsely normal if protein loss is slow; occult bleeding may be missed if stool occult blood is not repeated.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain or distension, haematemesis, persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss, jaundice, or signs of sepsis

faq.q: What is the most common indication for gastrectomy in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Gastric cancer and peptic ulcer disease, often related to H. pylori infection.

faq.q: Why are proton‑pump inhibitors used after gastrectomy?
faq.a: They reduce acid secretion, preventing ulceration at the anastomosis and improving nutritional absorption.

faq.q: Can a patient develop dumping syndrome after a Billroth I?
faq.a: Yes, rapid gastric emptying into the duodenum can cause early dumping symptoms such as nausea, dizziness and diarrhoea.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with suspected gastric cancer? — Endoscopy with biopsy to confirm malignancy and assess depth of invasion.
A patient presents with early satiety and weight loss after a Billroth II. What complication should you suspect? — Dumping syndrome; look for post‑prandial hypoglycaemia and diarrhoea.

During a ward round you notice a patient with a recent subtotal gastrectomy has a sudden drop in haemoglobin. What is the most urgent step? — Check for anastomotic leak with clinical exam and, if available, CT or bedside ultrasound; start resuscitation.
Why are NSAIDs contraindicated in a post‑gastrectomy patient? — They increase gastric mucosal bleeding risk and impair healing of the anastomosis.
A patient develops bile reflux gastritis after a Billroth II. What pharmacological treatment is most appropriate? — Proton‑pump inhibitor to reduce acid and protect mucosa.
You are asked to counsel a patient on diet after a total gastrectomy. What key point should you emphasise? — Small, frequent meals low in fat and fibre to prevent dumping and optimise absorption.
What is the recommended surveillance interval for stump cancer after a partial gastrectomy? — Endoscopy at 6–12 months post‑op, then annually if normal.
You observe a patient with post‑gastrectomy protein loss. Which drug can help reduce protein loss? — Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, reduces splanchnic protein loss.
